item.title: Attack on University of Texas Students Tests Texas G.O.P. Unity
item.description:
Gov. Greg Abbott of Texas gathered top Republicans candidates around him over the summer for a photo portrait in a display of party unity following a bruising primary. There was Ken Paxton, running for U.S. Senate, and Dan Patrick, the lieutenant governor.

And there, smiling over Mr. Abbott’s right shoulder, was Bo French.

At the time, few outside Texas politics were familiar with Mr. French, a candidate for a statewide office regulating oil and gas who has a history of unvarnished bigotry.

But over the weekend he rocketed to national attention — almost all of it negative — after posting racist attacks on University of Texas students as they enjoyed a moment of pure elation at their football team’s improbable comeback victory. In one post, Mr. French described South Asian students at the school as “foreigners” who had “displaced” Americans at the state’s flagship university.

Mr. French’s posts struck a chord in a way his anti-immigrant and anti-Muslim comments have not before. The messages threatened to fracture the Texas Republicans’ attempts at solidarity and tested their willingness to criticize one of their own — just weeks before midterm voting begins. Mr. French denied his posts were racist and threw the blame back on Republicans who didn’t fully support his message.

The posts have also given Democrats renewed hope to win a statewide office in Texas for the first time in a generation. While much of the national focus has been on the U.S. Senate race against Mr. Paxton, the scandal-plagued attorney general running against James Talarico, state party officials believe Mr. French and another anti-immigrant hard-liner, Don Huffines, are particularly vulnerable. The hard-liners on the Republican slate may help Democrats in other races as well.

“There are certainly Republican candidates this cycle that are so outside of the mainstream that it provides opportunities for us,” said Kendall Scudder, the chairman of the Texas Democratic Party. A year ago, he added, those opportunities “may not have seemed possible.”

Recent polls show Mr. French with a slim lead over his Democratic opponent, Jon Rosenthal. Republicans had rallied around Mr. French, even if, like Mr. Abbott, they did not support him in the primary.

Last week, Mr. French projected confidence as he walked around President Trump’s midterm convention in Dallas.

“We are working together, all of us are working together to make sure we win,” he told The New York Times on Friday. When asked about Democrats believing he was an easy target, Mr. French said, “Let them think that.”

Then came his posts Sunday morning that drew condemnation from some of the party’s top elected officials and candidates running for office. But not all of them.

The speaker of the Texas House, Dustin Burrows, called on Mr. French to delete Sunday’s post. Senator John Cornyn, who lost in the primary to Mr. Paxton, urged Republicans to condemn Mr. French’s “intolerance and racism.” And Karl Rove, the former senior adviser to George W. Bush, is reported to have said he would vote for a Democrat for the first time in decades because of the incident.

Mr. Abbott chastised Mr. French for his divisive rhetoric while, in the same statement, saying he supported Texas having “the toughest immigration laws of any state in America.”

By contrast, Mr. Patrick, who had previously called for Mr. French’s resignation, said nothing about the post and did not comment.

Nate Sheets, who is running for agriculture commissioner, said in an interview with The Times that the proliferation of mosques and Hindu temples in Texas was “frustrating people,” and he criticized immigrant communities he said were not assimilating.

“He pointed out that a bunch of those students were Indian kids,” Mr. Sheets said, referring to Mr. French. “How he articulated that — no, I didn’t like that. Do I agree with the sentiment that the immigration system that we have in America today is creating a negative future for America? I do. I do agree with that.”

The split reaction to Mr. French’s posts gave him room to double down.

“Some of the less conservative people in Texas are the ones attacking me,” Mr. French said in a radio interview on Monday.

It was not the first time Republicans have criticized Mr. French for his social media posts.

Last summer, he received blowback after posting a poll on social media asking whether Jews or Muslims posed the bigger threat to America. He deleted the post, which he insisted was not antisemitic, and refused calls to resign as head of the Republican Party in Tarrant County, which includes Fort Worth.

In November, Mr. French said he would run for the state’s influential three-member oil and gas regulatory board, the Texas Railroad Commission.

Mr. Abbott, Mr. Patrick and Mr. Burrows, all backed Mr. French’s opponent in the Republican primary runoff, Jim Wright, the incumbent commissioner. Despite their opposition, Mr. French won. His victory did little to temper his combative social media presence.

In the past year, he has called people who believe in transgender rights or birthright citizenship “retards.” He described Native Americans as “third world savages, who were conquered.” He said he wanted to “denaturalize and deport” all Muslims in the United States.

Top Republicans in Texas did not respond to those posts as they did to the one attacking the University of Texas students.

Aside from Mr. French, another vulnerable down-ballot candidate is Mr. Huffines, who once challenged Mr. Abbott from the right.

Mr. Huffines, who Mr. Abbott installed as acting comptroller after his primary win, did not comment on Mr. French’s weekend post. Sarah Eckhardt, the Democrat in the race, said Mr. Huffines’s silence amounted to tacit approval.

“I have watched how this party has become more and more hard-line,” said Ms. Eckhardt, a state senator and former prosecutor. Mr. Huffines did not respond to request for comment.

Mr. Rosenthal said he knew he was in for a tough fight against Mr. French. A Democrat has not won a statewide race in Texas in more than 30 years.

“The odds are still against me,” Mr. Rosenthal said. He said he had received dozens of death threats from Mr. French’s supporters, some attacking him for being Jewish.

When asked about the antisemitism directed at his opponent, Mr. French told The Times at last week’s convention that Mr. Rosenthal was “not practicing Jewish.”

Mr. Rosenthal pushed back.

“Anyone that thinks it’s their job to pass judgment on whether I’m Jewish or not can shove it,” he said.

For his part, Mr. French has acted as though the bipartisan scorn his post elicited actually amounted to a win for him. On Monday evening, he thanked the “patriots” who just helped him cross 100,000 followers on X.

Then, he posted about his opponent being “radical.”

item.title: News Choppers Gathered in the Los Angeles Sky. Then One Fell to Earth.
item.description:
The collision of the bus and the S.U.V. had been big, even by Los Angeles eye-in-the-sky standards. Desmond Shaw was stunned by its force.

Mr. Shaw, a veteran helicopter reporter in a sprawling city that has long looked to the air for news, had gazed at the wreck from above, transfixed. His aircraft was one in a swarm of choppers hovering high over the San Fernando Valley on Tuesday. The transit vehicle had been bashed like a toy, the S.U.V. jammed into its midsection. Authorities were saying at least two people were dead and many more were injured or trapped.

Mr. Shaw, a 45-year-old who works for a CBS affiliate, was back at work less than a week after taking a family leave prompted by the deaths of both parents, and he had been thinking lately about mortality. The crash was eerie for him, and he was glad to be done with the story.

But as he and his pilot were flying away, the newsroom called back: An aircraft appeared to have gone down nearby.

He thought of his fellow reporters aloft — colleagues for whom the air was their office.

“As soon as we got there and saw the fireball and the rotor blades, we knew what it was,” he said, speaking in an interview from his car early Wednesday. “It was the day we all dread.”

The back-to-back bus and helicopter crashes killed five people and strewed blackened wreckage in the Chatsworth neighborhood of Los Angeles. The bus crash happened shortly after 5 p.m. when the S.U.V. broadsided a Los Angeles Metro bus, killing at least two people and critically injuring others.

Then, around 7 p.m., a helicopter reporting for a local NBC affiliate plummeted to the ground and burst into flames. The reporter, Eliana Moreno, and the pilot, George Marciniw, were killed, along with a person on the ground.

The helicopter was just one of a fleet that zips over Southern California’s vastness, tracking events like car chases and wildfires, most of them supplied by contractors who provide aircraft and reporters to news stations.

The choppers, swashbuckling and loud, are a signature of the region, indispensable in a metropolis encompassing thousands of square miles. The crash on Tuesday night of an aircraft attempting to cover a spectacular collision, however, underscored another aspect of Los Angeles’s aerial news culture: the risks.

Helicopter crews across the United States say they must remain on constant lookout for hazards such as drones and bird strikes, as well as pilot error and mechanical failure. Although driving on freeways is statistically more dangerous than air travel, the crash of a tourist chopper in the Hudson River last year and the 2020 accident that killed the N.B.A. legend Kobe Bryant, his 13-year-old daughter and seven others have highlighted the long odds of surviving a helicopter accident.

At least eight fatal crashes involving news helicopters have occurred in the United States since 2000, killing 16 people, federal accident records and news accounts show.

In Los Angeles, two people were seriously injured in 2000 when a news helicopter covering the Academy Awards crashed at Van Nuys Airport.

At NBC4, formally known as KNBC, Tuesday’s tragedy summoned the memory of the 1977 helicopter crash that killed the KNBC correspondent Francis Gary Powers. A reconnaissance plane pilot, Mr. Powers had survived being shot down over the Soviet Union during the Cold War only to perish on his way back from covering a wildfire.

In the interview, Mr. Shaw said that helicopter journalists have to put aside their fears.

“You have to push it to the back of your brain or you can’t do the job,” he said. “I had a fear of heights when I was a kid. Now I’m sometimes up 10,000 feet high.”

Mr. Shaw has worked in broadcasting since his college days at California State University, Northridge, where he was news anchor for the campus radio station. He later became that most specific of Los Angeles media figures: a radio traffic reporter. For more than a decade, he flew above the freeways, keeping motorists apprised of hazards, from “gawker’s block” to jackknifed big rigs, as well as the occasional disaster or wildfire.

He joined CBS LA in 2015, and has been a full-time reporter and cameraman there for six years. He said he was well acquainted with Ms. Moreno and Mr. Marciniw.

“We knew pretty quickly who it was,” he said. “It’s a pretty tight knit community. There are probably a dozen of us, or maybe less, who report on air and run the camera.”

NBC4 said on Tuesday that its NewsChopper4 had been operated by a team from a Los Angeles-based vendor, Angel City Air. Mr. Shaw had run into them at airports over the years as they covered breaking stories, he said, and knew their voices by heart from broadcasts. So did the other reporters hovering overhead when the crash happened, and who have since heard the audio clips circulating on social media that are said to be their last communications.

“Heartbreaking doesn’t begin to describe it,” he said.

Mr. Shaw and his pilot didn’t see the crash, only the devastation on the ground in Chatsworth. The hours since have been a blur, he said: speaking on the air with his station’s news anchors and reassuring his loved ones that he was all right.

He took time in his car for one last interview before going home to greet his dogs, Lonzo and Scruffy, and hug his husband, Brandon. His phone, he said, had been sounding off all night with messages of concern and condolence.

“Everyone is asking if I’m OK,” he said. “Honestly? No. But I’m alive.”

item.title: What We Know About the Victims in the L.A. Helicopter Crash
item.description:
Two of the people killed in Los Angeles on Tuesday in a helicopter crash were a journalist and pilot who had flown hundreds of hours together since they first teamed up in 2023.

A third person on the ground was killed in the crash, which followed a bus accident that the news helicopter was covering when it went down.

At least two people were killed, and several others critically injured, when an S.U.V. slammed into a Los Angeles Metro bus in Chatsworth, a neighborhood in the San Fernando Valley, on Tuesday evening. About two hours later, the helicopter, which NBC4 Los Angeles said was operated by Angel City Air, plummeted to the ground nearby.

The identities of many of the victims were still unknown on Wednesday.

Here’s what we know about the victims.

Ms. Moreno, who was in her late 30s, was on board the helicopter when it crashed on Tuesday, according to NBC4.

She was born in Orange County, Calif., just south of Los Angeles, and studied broadcast journalism and political science at Chapman University, graduating in 2010, the station said.

Mr. Moreno had known she wanted to be a television news reporter since she was 11 years old, according to her LinkedIn profile. She went by “Eli in the heli” on social media and NBC4 described her as a “seasoned aerial journalist” who had covered “countless police pursuits” and other news events.

She also reported in Spanish, providing coverage for Telemundo 52, the Spanish-language sister channel of NBC4.

In a post on social media in 2023, she described her work as “the best job in the world.”

She is survived by her fiancé, Robert Barrientos, the station said. The pair were engaged in 2025, according to a post she shared on social media.

In a joint statement, NBC4 and Telemundo 52 said they were “deeply saddened” by the crash. “We extend our heartfelt condolences to the families, friends and colleagues of those who lost their lives,” the statement said.

Mr. Marciniw was at the controls of the helicopter when it crashed on Tuesday, NBC4 said.

He grew up in Southern California and graduated in 1974 from Burbank High School, about 11 miles northwest of downtown Los Angeles, according to the station. His father, Petro Marciniew, who died in 2015, was born in Ukraine and emigrated to the United States, where he worked as a cabinet maker, according to an online obituary.

Mr. Marciniw had worked in helicopter flight services for nearly 40 years, according to his Facebook profile. He had also been a helicopter flight instructor for more than 30 years, according to an online profile offering his services as an instructor.

Mr. Marciniw, who went by “Whirly dude” on Instagram, frequently posted images taken during his flights above Los Angeles, including those with Ms. Moreno. “And thats a wrap for Friday night as the heavy fog rolls in with Eliana Moreno,” he wrote in a caption for a photo he posted of the NBC4 News helicopter.

In December 2025, he posted a selfie on Facebook with Ms. Moreno in front of the same helicopter. “Eliana and I wishing everyone a Merry Christmas and Happy Holidays as we look forward to the start of a New Year,” he wrote.

item.title: Officer Sues Capitol Police, Alleging Racial Bias
item.description:
A veteran U.S. Capitol Police officer who responded to the Jan. 6, 2021, attack and has overseen multiple units sued the agency on Wednesday, alleging that she was passed over for a promotion as part of a push to eliminate racial and gender diversity on the force.

The officer, Carneysha Mendoza, a Black woman and Army veteran, said in a complaint filed in Federal District Court in Washington that the Capitol Police are “engaged in an effort to reverse diversity, equity and inclusion gains and eliminate diversity in leadership within the department.”

Her lawsuit is the latest in a string of discrimination allegations in recent years against the department, which has paid out nearly $1 million since 2022 to settle employment claims, according to public reports and court records reviewed by The New York Times.

Ms. Mendoza, who has served with the Capitol Police for 24 years and held supervisory roles in four of its six bureaus, was passed over for the role of deputy chief, as well as three assistant chief positions. Two of those roles were awarded to officers who had been reprimanded for serious disciplinary infractions, according to her complaint, including a white male officer who was disciplined for “serious offenses including drunk driving” on the job and overtime fraud.

Ms. Mendoza testified before the House committee investigating the Jan. 6 attack that she had come into work early that day and “jumped on line” with her co-workers to hold off crowds of rioters pressing their way into the Capitol, sustaining chemical burns to her face.

In the complaint on Wednesday, she said the current Capitol Police chief, Michael G. Sullivan, who assumed office in June 2025, had disbanded the department’s office of equity and inclusion that August. He later sent a facilities employee “to collect and destroy all” materials created by the office, including some materials she kept in her office.

“When Inspector Mendoza asked Chief Sullivan about the incident, he stated that his instructions were that the materials would be removed from her office overnight, when no one would be present,” the complaint says.

The Times analysis shows that the Capitol Police have paid out nearly $1 million since 2022 for claims filed under the law that provides employment protections to legislative employees.

A spokesman for the Capitol Police, Tim Barber, declined on Wednesday to comment on Ms. Mendoza’s case or the other discrimination claims brought against the department by employees.

The suit comes as the department has struggled to hire and retain staff. Mr. Sullivan told lawmakers during a March budget hearing that staffing shortages “span all operational units.” The force has requested a budget of more than $1 billion for the coming fiscal year, a 20 percent increase.

Last year in another case, a Washington jury found that a female officer had been removed from a K-9 training program because of her gender — even as her male counterparts were improperly advanced after they failed to identify explosive materials during examinations.

A jury awarded her damages of $850,000, though the amount was ultimately lowered to $300,000 to comply with a statutory limit.

In that case, the officer, Mauricia VanMeter, was removed from a training program for poor performance, though video footage of training exercises and certification examinations showed that she had performed better than some of her male counterparts, according to court transcripts.

Kenneth Hill, the Capitol Police K-9 trainer, testified that one of Ms. VanMeter’s male counterparts in the program should have been disqualified after he made multiple mistakes during a certification exam meant to demonstrate the ability to work with a dog to detect explosive devices or chemicals.

Instead, he was certified. Mr. Hill also testified that he intervened during that test to help the male officer avoid making additional mistakes.

“You also falsified the records to make it look like his performance wasn’t so bad, didn’t you?” asked Les Alderman, Ms. VanMeter’s lawyer.

“I guess,” Mr. Hill replied.

Mr. Hill also agreed that supervisors within his unit “completely reorganized” part of a certification exam for a second male officer after his dog was unable to pass an odor recognition test in a warehouse. Mr. Hill said that the dog in question was not trained to identify odors in such an environment and was only meant to identify improvised explosive devices in luggage.

“If a bad guy with a bomb decided to go into a warehouse and” the officer in question “was on duty that day, what would they do, call someone else?” Mr. Alderman asked.

“No,” Mr. Hill replied.

Mr. Barber also declined to comment on Mr. Hill or his testimony.

In a separate 2023 case convened by the Office of Congressional Workplace Rights, both an administrative hearing officer and an appeals board found that the Capitol Police discriminated and retaliated against a Black training supervisor in the K-9 unit, and replaced him with a white officer with “objectively inferior qualifications.”

The officer, Juan Cobbin, was removed from his position as head of K-9 training and transferred to a non-K-9 position at the Library of Congress. That was after he had complained to his supervisors and the department’s office of professional responsibility about “racially tinged” emails written by white K-9 officers in their capacity as union members.

The emails “unfairly singled out African American supervisors for criticism, expressly referred to him as ‘a joke,’ and stated that he should not be listened to by his U.S.C.P. leadership on matters such as the deployment of canines during Black Lives Matters protests and the insurrection of Jan. 6, 2021,” according to hearing documents.

Mr. Cobbin was awarded $125,000 in emotional pain and suffering damages as well as about $30,000 in economic damages.

Kitty Bennett contributed research.

item.title: House Holds Leon Black in Contempt Over Epstein Subpoenas
item.description:
The House on Wednesday unanimously agreed to hold the billionaire investor Leon Black in criminal contempt of Congress after he refused to appear for a deposition and turn over documents to a key panel investigating the disgraced financier and sex offender Jeffrey Epstein.

The citation, agreed to without a recorded vote, amounts to an official recommendation that the Justice Department bring federal charges against Mr. Black. It may serve to refocus public attention on the Trump administration’s handling of investigative material related to Mr. Epstein just as lawmakers depart Washington for a final spate of campaigning before the midterm congressional elections.

While President Trump has labored to avoid discussing the Epstein matter and excoriated those clamoring for more transparency, Republicans in Congress have tried to show they take the case, which has generated outrage among their core supporters, seriously.

The House Oversight Committee issued subpoenas to Mr. Black in June, after he refused to answer questions about nondisclosure agreements that he had signed with women, some of whom had been linked to Mr. Epstein. The panel demanded that he appear for a deposition and provide copies of any nondisclosure agreements he might have entered into. Mr. Black refused to comply and instead sued the committee, accusing it of exceeding its authority.

The committee on Tuesday unanimously recommended holding Mr. Black in contempt. Representative James R. Comer, Republican of Kentucky and the panel’s chairman, accused him of using the lawsuit as cover.

“Mr. Black is hiding behind litigation to delay having to provide answers to the American people,” he said on Tuesday. “No one is above the law. Mr. Black will be treated the same as anyone else in this investigation, and his actions have consequences.”

Representative Robert Garcia of California, the top Democrat on the committee, said in an interview that Mr. Black had clearly violated two subpoenas.

“Subpoenas have to mean something in the Congress,” he said. “When you give $180 million to Jeffrey Epstein and are unwilling to answer questions about why and where and how you were involved? I think that’s a huge, huge issue.”

Mr. Black’s lawyers, Susan Estrich and Aaron Cutler, criticized the contempt vote in a statement, saying that Mr. Comer’s actions were “politically motivated and completely retaliatory.” They said that Mr. Black had already provided the committee with the “only confidentiality agreement” that was relevant to its investigation. They also said they had filed an ethics complaint against Mr. Comer, though they declined to specify what offenses they believed he had committed.

Mr. Black’s lawsuit said that the Oversight Committee’s subpoenas were “invalid” and that unnamed women and others “whom he has or may have agreements” with had “bargained for confidentiality.” Those people “want no association with the Epstein scandal,” the lawsuit said.

Mr. Black paid Mr. Epstein $170 million from 2013 to 2017 for what he described as traditional tax and estate planning services, according to congressional records and government documents.

Mr. Black has repeatedly said he knew nothing about Mr. Epstein’s decades-long sexual abuse of teenage girls and young women. But the release of millions of pages of emails and documents by the Justice Department put a new focus on Mr. Epstein’s relationship with Mr. Black.

Mr. Epstein advised Mr. Black on how to address issues he faced with several women with whom Mr. Black had sexual affairs. And Mr. Black paid about $20 million to a dozen women, according to the files and notes taken by congressional investigators that were previously shared with The New York Times.

item.title: Susie Wiles, Trump’s Chief of Staff, Says She Is ‘Cancer Free’
item.description:
Susie Wiles, President Trump’s chief of staff, said that she was “cancer free” after an appointment at the Mayo Clinic this week, following a diagnosis of breast cancer earlier this year.

“After a medical appointment at the Mayo Clinic this week, my pathology results came back clear,” Ms. Wiles, 69, said on social media, adding: “Thank you to my family, friends, doctors, and everyone who prayed for me, checked in, and supported me along the way. A special thank you to President Trump for his unwavering support.”

Ms. Wiles, the first woman to hold the chief of staff role at the White House, had disclosed the diagnosis in March and said the disease was caught in its early stages. She said she would remain in her job during treatment.

Ms. Wiles did not identify the specific treatment course she underwent. In recent years, there have been significant advances in breast cancer treatments, particularly if the disease is caught in earlier stages. The Mayo Clinic, which Ms. Wiles visited this week, is one of the nation’s premier medical systems.

Ms. Wiles has been a key figure for Mr. Trump in the past five years. She oversaw Mr. Trump’s political operation and the 2024 campaign that returned him to the White House. Ms. Wiles was one of two senior members of Mr. Trump’s campaign, along with his longtime aide Dan Scavino, traveling with the president when he was shot in his right ear during an outdoor rally in Butler, Pa., on July 13, 2024.

item.title: Newsom Signs Jay Leno’s Classic Car Bill Over Environmentalist Objections
item.description:
Vintage car enthusiasts won a reprieve from California’s strict emissions rules after a push led by the comedian and classic car collector Jay Leno.

Gov. Gavin Newsom announced on Wednesday that he had signed legislation exempting classic cars made before the model year 1981 from state smog checks that measure pollution levels. He also signed a bill to create a specialty license plate commemorating lowrider vehicles.

“These bills protect a treasured part of California culture, giving car owners a way to preserve these pieces of history for generations to come,” Mr. Newsom said in a statement.

The governor’s announcement was accompanied by a video of him touring Mr. Leno’s classic car garage in Burbank, Calif. It shows the men strolling past a collection that includes a 1957 Buick Roadmaster, a 1966 Chevrolet Corvair, a 1989 Bentley Turbo R and a fleet of open-wheel roadsters and vintage British sports cars.

Environmentalists opposed the measure for weakening pollution controls that have helped reduce smog, and a similar bill stalled last year.

Mr. Newsom has repeatedly pushed for Californians to embrace electric vehicles and signed an executive order phasing out the sale of new gas-powered cars in California. He has boasted that the state’s regulations helped spur the creation of Tesla. But as he nears the end of his tenure as governor in January and considers a potential run for president, Mr. Newsom may be positioning himself to appeal to a broader electorate.

California law generally requires a smog check every two years for gas-powered vehicles from the 1976 model year and beyond. Mr. Leno and other car collectors argued that the rule was too strict and said that it was difficult to find mechanics who had the equipment necessary to run a smog check on older cars. They lobbied for an exemption and set up a display of classic vehicles outside the State Capitol in Sacramento as they worked to make their case in August.

The new law, which proponents nicknamed “Leno’s Law” after the comedian, says owners must have collector-car insurance or prove that their vehicle is driven fewer than 1,000 miles per year to qualify for the exemption. It takes effect on Jan. 1, 2028, and will be phased in over five years, eventually exempting collector cars made before the 1986 model year.

“This is a big day for California’s car community,” Mr. Leno said on social media. “We’re preserving a piece of automotive history while recognizing that a collector car isn’t the same thing as a daily driver.”

Environmentalists lobbied against the bill, arguing that relaxing the smog check rules would make air pollution worse and could harm health conditions such as asthma. It passed the California Legislature with bipartisan support, though many Democrats objected to the proposal.

item.title: U.S. Charges Five Men in Russia-Backed Assassination Plots
item.description:
Federal prosecutors have accused five men of being part of a network that planned to assassinate Russian dissidents and others in the United States and abroad. The charges say that the plots were orchestrated by the Kremlin.

The indictment, unsealed on Tuesday in U.S. District Court for the Southern District of New York, said three of the defendants were members of the Russian intelligence services: Yuri Khrameev, 63; his son Kirill Khrameev, 27; and Oemis Romagoza Durruthy, 35, a Cuban national living in Russia who prosecutors said coordinated attacks for the network.

Yaidel Delgado Suarez, 35, was a recruiter for the network who tried to find people in the United States for “surveillance and murder,” according to the indictment. It said Mr. Suarez, Yuri Khrameev and the fifth defendant, Angel Eduardo Castro, 22, recruited a person in the United States to kill “a prominent Russian dissident” who the network believed was living in the Washington, D.C., area. The dissident was not named in the indictment.

The five defendants are charged with conspiracy to finance terrorism. Yuri Khrameev, Mr. Suarez and Mr. Castro also face a charge of conspiracy to commit murder for hire, according to the indictment.

Asked on Wednesday about the indictment, the Kremlin’s spokesman, Dmitri S. Peskov, said at a scheduled briefing, “Until we have heard and seen any coherent evidence and arguments based on something tangible, we do not consider it necessary to comment.”

The defendants were not in custody, according to a statement from the U.S. attorney’s office in Manhattan. It was not immediately clear if they had lawyers.

In addition to the Russian dissident in the U.S., the network’s targets included civilian and military infrastructure in Europe, according to the indictment.

“As alleged, the defendants, working for the intelligence services of Russia, conspired to cause destruction and mayhem around the world, including right here in the United States,” James M. McDonald, the U.S. attorney for the Southern District of New York, said in the statement.

The prosecutors’ indictment described the defendants’ recruiting efforts for surveillance and murder plots that unfolded in 2024, 2025 and in the summer of this year.

One involved efforts this July to recruit someone to kill the dissident. The indictment said Mr. Suarez sent Mr. Castro, a citizen of Venezuela living in Russia, a voice message expressing the need to “measure a plot of land and provide measurements” for “construction” — coded language for surveillance and murder.

In two other voice messages to Mr. Castro, according to the indictment, Mr. Suarez said $1,000 to $1,500 would be paid for a video of an address and location belonging to someone they “want to eliminate, they want to disappear,” offering “$40,000 for whoever does the work.” In late July, Mr. Castro forwarded the messages to a Venezuelan citizen in Brooklyn, who expressed willingness to take “pics” but not do “the other stuff.”

Mr. Suarez later sent another location, provided by Yuri Khrameev, to the man in Brooklyn, who was paid after sending the videos and photographs to Mr. Suarez, it said.

Mr. Suarez then asked the man if he had “someone who wants to do construction” or if he would be interested in doing it himself.

The man offered to find someone else in three days, the indictment said.

Mr. Suarez tried to recruit other people over encrypted messaging applications and offered to pay them to kill the dissident and other victims in the United States, the indictment said.

In June 2025, Kirill Khrameev met an American at the Estonia-Russia border and paid the person $200 to photograph an address in Vilnius, the capital of Lithuania, the indictment said. He then put the American in touch with his father, Yuri Khrameev, who asked the recruit to kill a person associated with the address who was “telling the media and the common people that the Russians are the aggressors,” the indictment said.

The method could be “throwing a bottle of gasoline” or by “sticking a knife” in the victim, and the pay for doing so would be about $25,000, Mr. Khrameev told the recruit, as described in the indictment.

When the recruit declined, Mr. Khrameev offered a “simpler job,” which could include targeting and setting fires at military and civilian facilities in NATO countries and “all the countries that are helping Ukraine,” Mr. Khrameev said, according to the indictment.

The indictment also accused the Cuban defendant, Mr. Durruthy, of coordinating travel, payments and surveillance for the network in 2024, including for an attack in Prague and another one in Lithuania at a manufacturer of mobile radio stations intended for the Ukrainian military.

“These defendants allegedly operated as part of a global assassination network that reached into the United States, attempting to recruit U.S. citizens and foreigners to carry out killings at the behest of the Kremlin,” the assistant attorney general for national security, John A. Eisenberg, said in the statement.

Valerie Hopkins contributed reporting.

item.title: Senate Takes Up Bill to Regulate ‘Wild West’ of Collegiate Sports
item.description:
The Senate is considering legislation that would impose sweeping new standards across collegiate sports and limit the ability of top athletes to jump from school to school, wading into a politically charged issue with billions of dollars at stake.

In a strong bipartisan vote, senators agreed on Tuesday to open debate on the Protect College Sports Act, which would establish rules on payments to athletes, provide limited antitrust protection to the N.C.A.A. and set a five-year eligibility window for those playing college sports.

Its backers say it is needed to restore stability to a chaotic environment in which universities engage in bidding wars in what is known as the transfer portal, where top athletes exercise their leverage in pursuit of more compensation, winning records and different coaches.

“Right now, it is the Wild West,” said Senator Ted Cruz, Republican of Texas and a chief author of the measure with Senator Maria Cantwell, Democrat of Washington. He said the legislation would ensure that college sports “remain strong and vibrant for decades to come.”

The bill has also drawn opposition from members of both parties, and faces deep resistance from organized labor and civil rights groups. Opponents contend that the measure would limit the ability of athletes to be financially rewarded for their skills and allow schools and coaches to continue cashing in.

“What this bill does at its core is to protect a system of exploitation,” said Senator Chris Murphy, Democrat of Connecticut and a chief opponent of the legislation. He said the “chaos” being alleged by the bill’s backers is mainly an issue with coaches who have to work harder to retain athletes and recruit new ones, at a time when college sports are more popular and lucrative than ever.

“This bill protects the billions of dollars that coaches and sports industry executives are making over the suppression of compensation for some of the most highly valued athletes in the world,” Mr. Murphy said.

Civil rights groups have also registered strong objections, saying that Black and other minority athletes deserve to be treated fairly and share in the financial benefits reaped by schools from the sports programs that rely on their participation. Members of the Congressional Black Caucus oppose the legislation, and all five Black members of the Senate voted against putting it on the floor.

“Sharecropping is over,” Derrick Johnson, the president and chief executive of the N.A.A.C.P., said this week on a media call organized by the A.F.L.-C.I.O. “We should not ask athletes, particularly Black athletes, to generate revenue on the football field or basketball court and they share in none of the revenue.”

The furor over collegiate sports grew out of a series of court rulings, including by the Supreme Court, that resulted in college athletes being able to earn compensation for their “name, image and likeness,” or N.I.L. The N.C.A.A. had barred such compensation until it was forced under pressure to change its rules to allow athletes to accept paid endorsement deals. Then, in 2024, the N.C.A.A. changed a rule that had tightly restricted how and when college athletes could move between schools, leading to substantial annual turnover on the rosters of major teams.

Even some lawmakers who back the legislation questioned whether Congress should focus on college athletics weeks before a midterm election in which economic issues have been a primary concern. But Senator John Thune, Republican of South Dakota and the majority leader, had promised the bill’s backers a vote on whether to bring the legislation to the floor after an August recess.

The 74-to-24 vote to proceed was an unusual one in the polarized Senate, dividing both parties. Forty-nine Republicans, 24 Democrats and one independent backed moving forward with the bill. Nineteen Democrats, one independent and four Republicans opposed it.

The legislation takes aim at complex issues that have been litigated and relitigated in courts around the country. It has broad support from major athletic conferences, professional sports leagues, Olympians and prominent coaches, as well as strong backing from President Trump.

Ms. Cantwell, who said the legislation kept the door open to future collective bargaining rights for athletes, added that the current system was threatening the fiscal stability of many institutions struggling to keep up with the financial demands.

“The statistics show that the majority of college athletic departments right now can’t make ends meet,” Ms. Cantwell said, citing a “runaway arms race” in sports spending.

The legislation would guarantee the right to N.I.L. compensation. It would allow one college transfer and require that athletes sit out a year with a second move, though there would be exceptions, such as if a player’s coach were to quit, or if a sport were to be eliminated. The bill also limits midseason coaching moves.

Senator Chris Coons, a Delaware Democrat who helped negotiate the bill, said multiple new protections for student athletes had been added, including scholarship guarantees, extended health coverage and a 5-percent cap on payments to agents.

“I agree that college athletes deserve their rightful share of the revenue of college athletics, because they are the ones risking their health and taking a beating on the field,” he said. “But if we don’t get some stability in place by dealing with the eligibility problems, the transfer portal and the skyrocketing payments to coaches and athletes, we’re not going to have college sports within another year or two.”

But Senator Cory Booker, Democrat of New Jersey and a former Stanford football player, was not persuaded. He said the legislation unfairly restricted compensation for players, but not coaches.

“It is doing all kinds of things to stop players from earning money, putting bureaucracy between them and the possibility, but it does nothing to affect coaches,” Mr. Booker said. He noted that coaches at public universities were often the highest-paid public employees in their states.

“This is an unjust bill,” he said.

item.title: Merriam-Webster Dictionary Is Wordsmaxxing With 1,400 New Definitions
item.description:
Merriam-Webster, the venerable dictionary that traces its roots to a time before looksmaxxing and yacht rock, has added those words along with chili crisp, shapewear and cuffing season, to its comprehensive accounting of the English language.

The company, based in Springfield, Mass., announced on Tuesday that it had added those five terms and 1,395 other new definitions to its online dictionary, Merriam-Webster.com. Many will also be added to upcoming editions of the print dictionary.

Merriam-Webster is the oldest dictionary publisher in America. It traces its start to 1843, when the brothers George and Charles Merriam bought the rights to the 1841 edition of Noah Webster’s dictionary. The company emphasizes that the dictionary is not a static catalog, but a reflection of the many different ways words are used by real people.

That includes food-related words that have become more commonly used in the United States like superfood, “a food (such as salmon, broccoli, or blueberries) that is rich in nutrients,” and shishito, “a slender usually mild chili pepper of East Asia.” On the sweeter side, the dictionary added cake pop, “a compressed ball of cake crumbs and icing that is dipped in a usually chocolate or sugary coating,” for the uninitiated.

Anyone who dreads going to work or school might be familiar with the Sunday scaries, the “feelings of anxiety or sadness that arise on Sunday from the knowledge that the weekend is almost over.” And people who know Braden Peters, the proudly vain social media influencer known as Clavicular, might be familiar, for better or worse, with looksmaxxing. Merriam-Webster calls it “the practice of taking one or more sometimes extreme or dangerous measures intended to increase one’s physical attractiveness.”

Gregory Barlow, the president of Merriam-Webster, who declined to provide a complete list of the 1,400 new definitions added to the dictionary, said that the company did not remove any words in its latest update.

“There wasn’t a theme, but we can see that online culture and social media increasingly generate new language,” he said in an email. “Conversation on social platforms creates fertile soil in which new words crop up and spread.”

The process for keeping the dictionary up-to-date, or giving it a glow-up, which is one of the new terms just added, starts with editors who read widely and identify promising new entries for the dictionary. The editors then search through databases of articles, books and speeches, to see if those words have been used widely and have meanings that are broadly understood.

Proposed additions are reviewed by more senior colleagues, “but there’s no committee, no advocacy, no meetings for new word inclusion,” the company says on its website. Ultimately, it says, a word gets into the dictionary “when it is used by many people who all agree that it means the same thing.”

Merriam-Webster typically adds about 1,000 entries to the dictionary annually.

Fans of Christopher Cross, Kenny Loggins and Michael McDonald might be pleased to see that yacht rock made the cut. Merriam-Webster defines it as “a style of soft rock music originating in the 1970s and 1980s.”

Also clearing the bar was cuffing season, “a time of the year when people who are not married or in a relationship begin looking for a short-term romantic partner to spend the colder months of the year with.”

Merriam-Webster also added parasocial, “a one-sided emotional connection with someone (especially a celebrity or fictional character) whom one does not know personally,” and Rickroll, “to trick (someone) into hearing the song ‘Never Gonna Give You Up’ by English singer Rick Astley.”

“Words like cuffing season and looksmaxxing are widely used now, and people want to know what they mean, so we’re serving our audience by defining them,” Mr. Barlow said. “The online dictionary has limitless space to add all the words that merit inclusion, even if some words turn out to be relatively ephemeral.”

item.title: Democrats Put Aside Rifts With El-Sayed, Uniting to Win in Michigan
item.description:
Democratic senators from across the ideological spectrum huddled on Capitol Hill on Wednesday with Dr. Abdul El-Sayed, the progressive Senate nominee in Michigan and vocal critic of Israel, and said they were ready to put aside differences to win the majority in November.

More than a dozen Democrats flocked to the party’s political headquarters across from the Capitol to meet with Dr. El-Sayed and emerged sounding upbeat about a candidate who had not been the first choice of party leaders to defend the critical swing-state seat.

“He’s a great candidate,” Senator Kirsten Gillibrand of New York, the chairwoman of the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee, said after meeting with Dr. El-Sayed. “We haven’t lost Michigan in 30 years. He’s energizing the base, and I’m optimistic.”

Dr. El-Sayed, the Michigan-born son of Egyptian immigrants, won an expensive and competitive primary in Michigan last month that put on display deep divides within the Democratic Party. His past criticism of Israel — he has said he opposes Israel’s right to exist as a Jewish state — has continued to be a concern for Jewish Democratic voters in Michigan. Republicans are working to leverage that rift to boost his Republican opponent, former Representative Mike Rogers, in the general election.

The message from Democrats on Wednesday, however, was one of unity.

Senator Chris Murphy, Democrat of Connecticut, said that “Abdul is going to be able to cross over and get conservative, traditionally Republican support in Michigan. He’s more of a bridge-builder here than people think he will be. I’m all in.”

Senator Andy Kim, Democrat of New Jersey, who also met with Dr. El-Sayed, said that they connected as “dads just trying to make a better world for our little kids. We both know we’ve got a small window to make things right for them.”

And Senator Mark Kelly, Democrat of Arizona, emerged from the meeting saying that he planned to campaign in Michigan in the coming weeks.

Dr. El-Sayed also said he planned to meet with Senator Chuck Schumer, Democrat of New York and the minority leader, whom he has said he would not back as leader if he were to win in November. Mr. Schumer, the highest-ranking Jewish official in the country, often tells people his last name comes from the word “shomer,” meaning the guardian of Israel.

But Mr. Schumer reached out to Dr. El-Sayed following his victory and said he came away from the conversation believing “we have more that unites us than divides us.”

Dr. El-Sayed told reporters on Wednesday that he anticipated a “productive meeting” with the leader in which they would focus on areas of common ground.

“If Elon Musk or Donald Trump are out here trying to spend yet more money, I’m certainly hoping for future colleagues to support us,” Dr. El-Sayed said of the goal of his visit to Washington. “We need solidarity.”

He said Michigan voters were not concerned with his ties to Hasan Piker, the Twitch and YouTube star whose statements about Israel have alarmed Democrats.

“They really don’t care about that,” Dr. El-Sayed said. “Nobody asks me that question.”

His meetings with Democrats came a day after Vice President JD Vance encouraged Republicans on Capitol Hill to talk about Dr. El-Sayed, regardless of who they were running against, according to CNN.

Mr. Vance told House Republicans in a closed-door meeting that if they happened to be running against a Democrat who was “not that crazy, then just talk about Abdul El-Sayed.”

Dr. El-Sayed said he was unfazed by the attempt to turn him into a boogeyman of the far left.

“Fine, talk about me,” he said in response to the vice president. “You know what I’m going to talk about? Gas, groceries, how hard it is to see a doctor.”

item.title: Family of Woman Who Died While Pregnant Sues Texas Over Abortion Ban
item.description:
Days after a San Antonio emergency room sent Tierra Walker home with a diagnosis of pre-eclampsia in 2024, her son found her dead. It was his 15th birthday.

On Tuesday, Ms. Walker’s aunt Latanya Walker sued Attorney General Ken Paxton of Texas and others arguing that her death was a result of the state’s ban on abortions. Ms. Walker had sought an abortion, her lawyer said, because she didn’t expect to survive the pregnancy with her diagnosis.

The lawsuit filed in a state court in San Antonio is the latest challenge to Texas’ abortion ban, which remains one of the strictest in the nation. The suit argues that the law’s medical emergency exception exists only on paper and that doctors who invoke it risk prison, fines and the loss of their license.

Other lawsuits by women who say they were denied abortions despite grave risks to their lives or their fetuses have been dismissed or blocked by state courts.

The suit specifically names the sitting attorney general, Mr. Paxton, a Republican who is running for U.S. Senate; the head of the Texas Medical Board; the University of Texas Health Science Center at San Antonio and several doctors who treated her for complications during her pregnancy.

The lawsuit claims that Mr. Paxton’s office and medical leaders in the state created a climate of fear that affected the care Ms. Walker received. Doctors who perform an abortion outside the law’s narrow exception can face up to 99 years in prison, fines of at least $100,000 and the loss of their medical license.

The plaintiff is seeking an unspecified amount of money. The lawsuit also called the law unconstitutional because it deprived Ms. Walker of her right to live, Latanya Walker’s lawyers said.

Mr. Paxton’s office did not respond to a request for comment. Officials with the Texas Medical Board and the University of Texas Health Science Center at San Antonio declined to comment.

Mr. Paxton has filed several lawsuits against medical providers and medical organizations that prescribe and send abortion pills from states where abortion is legal to people in Texas.

The Texas law offers a narrow medical emergency exemption to save the life of the pregnant patient.

Ms. Walker died in 2024 after seeing many medical providers to help address pre-eclampsia, a severe high blood pressure condition in pregnancy that can be life threatening, and other health issues, lawyers for Latanya Walker said. She also suffered from pre-eclampsia in 2021 while pregnant with twins who were stillborn.

“Tierra Walker is proof that there is no exception because if she did not qualify, if even her doctors were too scared to act, then the medical emergency exception is nothing more than words on a page,” said Molly Duane, one of the attorneys.

Latanya Walker is being represented by Amplify Legal, the litigation arm of Abortion in America, an abortion rights advocacy group, and the Marynell Maloney Law Firm. The lawsuit claims that the abortion ban contributed to Ms. Walker’s death.

“For months, Ms. Walker had been asking for termination of her pregnancy — even though this was a wanted pregnancy — because she did not think she would survive the pregnancy. Tragically, she was right. An abortion at any point during her pregnancy would have saved her life,” the lawsuit said.

Ms. Walker, who was 37, left behind a teenage son and a husband.

Several other women have died after being denied or delayed pregnancy care under the state’s abortion restrictions, though the role of the law in individual cases remains contested. The full number of women in Texas who have died or suffered severe complications because of the restrictions is unknown.

The Texas Department of State Health Services announced this month that it would break with past precedent of releasing its biennial maternal mortality report in early September and wait until after the midterm elections in November. The report was expected to unveil the first set of data on maternal mortality since abortion became all but illegal in Texas.

Thirteen states ban abortion outright. Seven more states bar it after six to 12 weeks of pregnancy. The Supreme Court overturned Roe v. Wade in 2022, ending a federal constitutional right to abortion that had stood for nearly half a century.

Ms. Walker’s story gained widespread attention after a report by ProPublica.

Ms. Walker spent long stints at area hospitals and visited the emergency room several times during her pregnancy, where she underwent several tests. Despite the health risks, the lawsuit said none of the hospital staff advised her “on the possibility of abortion as a lifesaving medical treatment, offered her this treatment, or suggested that she leave the state.”

“Instead, hospital staff kept insisting ‘nothing is wrong with the baby’ and continued to refuse the care that she needed on that basis,” the lawsuit said.

She returned to the emergency room one last time on Dec. 27, 2024, where she was diagnosed with pre-eclampsia, but was discharged. Her teenage son found her dead days later.

“We want justice,” Latanya Walker said Wednesday during a news conference. “I don’t want this to happen to anyone else. This needs to stop.”

item.title: Sailors Admit to Dealing Fentanyl-Laced Pills on U.S.S. Abraham Lincoln
item.description:
Two former U.S. Navy service members pleaded guilty this week to selling counterfeit oxycodone pills containing fentanyl to active-duty sailors stationed in San Diego, including during their deployments, the Justice Department said.

The former sailors, Bailey A. Szramowski and Johnnese H. Poomaihealani, who are married and live in Hawaii, pleaded guilty on Monday in federal court in San Diego, where the aircraft carrier U.S.S. Abraham Lincoln is based. One sailor to whom Mr. Szramowski sold pills died of an overdose, and another was hospitalized, according to court records.

Mr. Szramowski, 29, provided an active-duty U.S. Navy service member assigned to the Lincoln with 10 such oxycodone pills in December 2022, court records show. The victim was identified by his initials A.N. in court records. He overdosed and died of acute fentanyl intoxication in January 2023.

At the time of his death, A.N. was on leave and staying in a recreational vehicle parked outside a home in San Leandro, Calif., that belonged to his aunt and uncle, records show.

Police officers said they found evidence of drug use at the scene, and a toxicology report indicated that A.N.’s blood had tested positive for the presence of fentanyl and THC, the psychoactive compound in cannabis. A.N.’s autopsy report concluded that he died of “acute fentanyl intoxication.”

Devastating losses. Drug overdose deaths, largely caused by the synthetic opioid drug fentanyl, reached record highs in the United States in 2021. Here’s what you should know to keep your loved ones safe:

Understand fentanyl’s effects. Fentanyl is a potent and fast-acting drug, two qualities that also make it highly addictive. A small quantity goes a long way, so it’s easy to suffer an overdose. With fentanyl, there is only a short window of time to intervene and save a person’s life during an overdose.

Stick to licensed pharmacies. Prescription drugs sold online or by unlicensed dealers marketed as OxyContin, Vicodin and Xanax are often laced with fentanyl. Only take pills that were prescribed by your doctor and came from a licensed pharmacy.

Talk to your loved ones. The best way to prevent fentanyl use is to educate your loved ones, including teens, about it. Explain what fentanyl is and that it can be found in pills bought online or from friends. Aim to establish an ongoing dialogue in short spurts rather than one long, formal conversation.

Learn how to spot an overdose. When someone overdoses from fentanyl, breathing slows and their skin often turns a bluish hue. If you think someone is overdosing, call 911 right away.

Buy naloxone. If you’re concerned that a loved one could be exposed to fentanyl, you may want to buy naloxone. The medicine can rapidly reverse an opioid overdose and is often available at pharmacies without a prescription. Narcan, the nasal spray version of naloxone, has received F.D.A. approval to be sold over the counter.

Ten days later, Mr. Szramowski sold three more pills to another sailor, identified as C.L., according to records.

That sailor was hospitalized for a suspected overdose and survived. Mr. Szramowski and Ms. Poomaihealani, 25, called C.L. and instructed C.L. to tell the authorities that the pills were from A.N., court records show.

Agents with the Naval Criminal Investigative Service also learned that Mr. Szramowski had asked A.N.’s aunt and uncle to delete the messages on A.N.’s phone between himself and A.N.

“My client is extremely remorseful for everything that happened, especially the death of A.N., who was a good friend of theirs,” a lawyer for Ms. Poomaihealani, Michael Littman, said on Wednesday. “She has accepted responsibility for her limited involvement in this case and is anxious to go forward with her life after her separation from the Navy.”

A lawyer for Mr. Szramowski was not immediately available for comment.

The U.S.S. Abraham Lincoln has been in the news this year. It left San Diego on Nov. 21 and spent roughly nine months at sea in the Persian Gulf, supporting U.S. operations against Iran, without a port call for its crew of about 5,000 sailors. The ship is now returning to its home port in Southern California after a stopover in Thailand.

Ultrapotent Street Drugs: Five decades after the “war on drugs” sought to make substance abuse unaffordable, illicit drugs are cheaper and more dangerous than ever. A visit to Baltimore shows why.

Fentanyl Tolerance: Habitual users of fentanyl have developed such a strong tolerance to the drug that standard doses of medications to manage withdrawal and initiate recovery are no longer working for many patients, a team of researchers in Los Angeles has found.

Overdose Deaths Drop: After years of relentless rises in overdose deaths, the United States has seen a remarkable reversal. The Trump administration is proposing to cut funding for many programs believed to have contributed to the improvement.

What to Know About Fentanyl: Tariffs intended to thwart the flow of fentanyl into the United States and dampen life-threatening overdoses tied to the drug have put fentanyl in the spotlight. Here’s what to know about the opioid.

C.L. told investigators that A.N. and Mr. Szramowski had been selling Percocet pills, which were most likely counterfeit, court records show, to other sailors for about a year. He said Mr. Szramowski sold the pills aboard the carrier during a 2022 deployment and after the ship returned to San Diego.

According to C.L., Mr. Szramowski bought the pills through the mail, using a post office box in Coronado, Calif. He then charged sailors for the pills through a mobile payment app.

An N.C.I.S. investigation of A.N.’s smartphone showed that from September through December 2022, Mr. Szramowski and A.N. regularly discussed drug use and drug sales — including “perc[s],” “coca,” “coke,” “blow,” “vics,” “hydrocodone,” “lsd,” “shrooms” and “ecstasy.” They also occasionally filmed themselves using drugs, according to the inquiry.

Mr. Szramowski faces five to 40 years in federal prison and a $5 million fine, while Ms. Poomaihealani faces up to 20 years and a $1 million fine, according to the Justice Department. They will be sentenced in December.

Kirsten Noyes contributed research.

item.title: Snubs, Flubs and Dueling Dan Sullivans: A Wild Primary Season Comes to a Close
item.description:
Primary season drew to a close in Delaware on Tuesday, ending seven unpredictable months that featured candidate switch-ups, nation-shaking upsets, debate debacles, and highs and lows for a vengeful president and each wing of a divided Democratic Party.

As we say farewell to the 2026 primaries, we are looking back at the candidates, races and moments that were so good, so bad or simply so strange that we won’t soon forget them.

The Republican Senate race in Texas. The testy race cost more than $130 million, according to the media tracking firm AdImpact, making it the most expensive Senate primary in years. Ken Paxton, the scandal-plagued Texas attorney general, won it with the backing of President Trump despite being outspent by roughly 8 to 1 on ads. Mr. Paxton defeated Senator John Cornyn, a longtime pillar of the Republican establishment and occasional critic of Mr. Trump. Mr. Paxton now faces James Talarico in a race that has Republicans nervous about holding the seat.

Senator Dan S. Sullivan of Alaska. That “S.” will be on the ballot because Senator Sullivan, a Republican running for re-election, is up against another candidate whose name has a familiar ring to it: Dan Sullivan. Alaska Republicans say that this Dan Sullivan — Dan J. Sullivan — was planted on the ballot by Democrats to confuse voters. Dan J. Sullivan says there’s no subterfuge, but he doesn’t campaign much. Democrats are hoping former Representative Mary Peltola can flip the seat.

Democrats. Seven Democratic members of Congress were ousted in primaries, as Democrats in many districts displayed a hunger for younger, more progressive candidates. Four of the incumbents lost to self-described democratic socialists. Four Republicans in the House were also defeated; the loss of Representative Thomas Massie of Kentucky, a fierce critic of Mr. Trump and the Iran war who became one of the president’s top targets, generated the most attention.

Republicans. Two Republican senators, who were each opposed by Mr. Trump, fell to primary challengers. Mr. Cornyn lost to Mr. Paxton in Texas, and Senator Bill Cassidy of Louisiana lost his primary after Mr. Trump backed a challenger, five years after Mr. Cassidy had voted to convict Mr. Trump in his second impeachment trial. No Democratic senators were unseated.

Troy Jackson, in Maine. Seventeen days passed between Mr. Jackson’s announcing that he was running for Senate in Maine and his winning the Democratic nomination at an unusual party convention. He was hastily selected to replace Graham Platner, the oysterman Maine Democrats had initially nominated. Mr. Platner exited the race after an accusation of rape, which he denied. Now Mr. Jackson, who lost in a bid for governor earlier this year, has a short window to make his case against Senator Susan Collins, who is one of the most vulnerable incumbent senators.

Senator Darline Graham of South Carolina. Ms. Graham, a political novice, had lived a quiet life near Columbia, S.C., before her older brother, Senator Lindsey Graham, died in July. Three days after his death, she was sworn in as a senator to serve the final months of his term. Then Ms. Graham, with Mr. Trump’s support, decided to run for a full term in November. With support from Mr. Trump and his super PAC, she narrowly won a runoff last month to secure the nomination. Just 45 days had passed since Mr. Graham’s death.

Ms. Graham. Mr. Graham was known for his interest in foreign affairs. But when Ms. Graham was asked about Taiwan at a debate, her answer drew gasps. “I’m just going to be honest here,” she replied. “I’m not that informed on national security.” She still won the race.

Republicans. Republicans won the redistricting war, which began last year when Mr. Trump urged Texas Republicans to take the rare step of redrawing House maps in the middle of the decade to create more safe Republican seats. Democrats tried to counter with their own gerrymanders. But aided by favorable rulings in state and federal courts, Republicans emerged with a national map that could help net them roughly five to 10 House seats.

Representative Haley Stevens of Michigan. Ms. Stevens, running for Senate in Michigan, was supported by Senator Chuck Schumer of New York, the minority leader, and Michigan’s governor, Gretchen Whitmer, a Democrat. Ms. Stevens also benefited from more than $60 million in advertising spending from several outside groups, including the super PAC arm of the American Israel Public Affairs Committee, the influential pro-Israel group. Still, Ms. Stevens was edged by Dr. Abdul El-Sayed, a progressive critic of Israel who was outspent by 9 to 1.

June. The Democratic Socialists of America shocked the political establishment. In New York City, two of its members, Darializa Avila Chevalier of Manhattan and Claire Valdez of Queens, won House primaries. A former D.S.A. member and self-described democratic socialist, Brad Lander of Brooklyn, defeated Representative Dan Goldman. And in Colorado, Melat Kiros, a 29-year-old democratic socialist, beat Representative Diana DeGette, a 15-term Democratic incumbent.

Francesca Hong. Ms. Hong, a democratic socialist running for governor in Wisconsin, went from improbable candidate to overwhelming primary favorite in the battleground state, in part because the moderate wing of the party failed to coalesce around a candidate. Still, Ms. Hong fell to a moderate, David Crowley, who had dropped out of the race for 10 days in the final weeks before the primary. (Her past dismissive words about Thanksgiving and other holidays may not have helped.) It was one of several big polling misses this primary season.

Ms. Stevens. Her strong Michigan accent briefly became a social media phenomenon, as amateur linguists debated her raised a’s and disappearing g’s.

May. Mr. Trump, flexing his hold on the Republican Party even as his overall approval rating flagged, ousted a number of Republican officials in May. He unseated Indiana state senators who had thwarted his redistricting efforts last year. He took down Mr. Cassidy and Mr. Massie within a four-day span. Mr. Cassidy did not even reach the runoff, and Mr. Massie, a seven-term incumbent, lost by about 10 points. And at the end of the month, his support helped Mr. Paxton beat Mr. Cornyn, whom Mr. Trump deemed insufficiently loyal. Although other candidates the president supported would go on to lose later, his streak in May showed his enduring sway with parts of his base.

Tom Smith, who dropped out but still won. Amir Hassan, a Navy veteran running for Congress in Michigan, had Mr. Trump’s powerful endorsement. His opponent, Mr. Smith, ran no ads, filed no campaign report, suspended his campaign and endorsed someone else. No matter. Voters in the Flint region chose Mr. Smith.

Florida’s Senate race. Angie Nixon, a democratic socialist in the state Legislature, ran on a shoestring budget in the Democratic Senate primary in Florida, which is known for its electorate’s antipathy toward socialism, in part because of its vibrant Latino population. Despite being vastly outspent, Ms. Nixon took down Alex Vindman, a moderate former national security official who gained national notice in 2019 after he was a top witness in Mr. Trump’s first impeachment trial. She called it a victory “for the little guys and girls.”

Scott Brown. Mr. Brown, a moderate Republican, shocked the political world when he managed to win Edward M. Kennedy’s old Senate seat in deep-blue Massachusetts in a 2010 special election. Mr. Brown lost two years later to Senator Elizabeth Warren, then tried for a Senate comeback this year in another state: New Hampshire. But Senator John E. Sununu of New Hampshire thrashed him in the Republican primary, winning by more than 40 points. Before the primary Mr. Brown said he had a vision for what he might do if he lost: “Work out, drink and go gamble and come home and take a nap for a day or two.”

“Life,” Mr. Brown said, “goes on.”

That’s true. And now the sprint to the general election begins.

Matt Zdun and Theodore Schleifer contributed reporting.

item.title: Congress Clears Russia Sanctions Bill, Sending It to Trump
item.description:
The House on Wednesday passed sweeping legislation intended to squeeze the financial lifelines sustaining Russia’s war against Ukraine, overcoming more than a year of resistance to send President Trump a measure that would slap tough new sanctions on Moscow and extend them against Iran.

The centerpiece of the measure would attack Russia’s energy sector, which has financed the assault on Ukraine. It would allow the president to impose tariffs of as much as 100 percent on countries, including China and India, that are among the top five purchasers of Russian oil or gas, and the top facilitators of the so-called shadow fleet of vessels used to evade restrictions on Russia’s oil exports.

Named for Senator Lindsey Graham, the South Carolina Republican who died in July after spending more than a year building support for the bill, it would also impose sanctions on Russian officials, oligarchs and financial institutions.

It was approved 262 to 159, clearing it for Mr. Trump, who has signaled he will sign it. Despite the strong bipartisan backing for punishing Russia, 152 Democrats opposed the legislation, contending that it gave too much new tariff authority to a president who has already gone around Congress repeatedly on trade matters.

The legislation includes a five-year extension of sanctions targeting Iran’s energy and weapons sectors, a reflection of the concern in Congress over the close military relationship between Moscow and Tehran.

Its final passage capped a turbulent journey through Congress for the bill, led by Mr. Graham and Senator Richard Blumenthal, Democrat of Connecticut. They first began the sanctions effort early last year and encountered early resistance from Mr. Trump, who did not want to allow Congress to tie his hands on dealing with Russia.

Before his death, Mr. Graham had been the key intermediary between Capitol Hill and the White House as officials in Washington debated competing approaches to economically isolating Russia. Mr. Graham secured the administration’s backing shortly before his death, clearing the way for the Senate to overwhelmingly approve the legislation last month.

Still, its path through the House also proved to be complicated.

Some Democrats who have been among Ukraine’s most vocal supporters balked at the tariff provisions, particularly after the Supreme Court curtailed some of Mr. Trump’s previous efforts to impose tariffs without explicit authorization from Congress. They warned that the president could use the new trade powers more broadly than Congress intended.

Representative Gregory W. Meeks of New York, the top Democrat on the Foreign Affairs Committee, said on Wednesday that Congress should instead provide Ukraine with additional military and humanitarian assistance while tightening restrictions on the president’s ability to waive sanctions.

“We can support Ukraine. We can hold Russia accountable,” Mr. Meeks said. “And we can protect the American people from higher costs.”

Supporters countered that the legislation explicitly restricts the new tariff authority to countries purchasing Russian energy or facilitating sanctions evasion, and maintained that the tariffs were essential because previous penalties had failed to sufficiently choke off Moscow’s energy revenues. The measure includes an exemption for certain countries that rely on Russian natural gas but are taking significant steps to reduce their dependence.

Representative Michael McCaul, Republican of Texas and one of the bill’s leading proponents, said the tariffs were “the teeth of this bill,” intended to force major buyers of Russian energy to choose between continued purchases from Moscow and access to the American market.

“You can evade sanctions, which the Russians have done for years, but you cannot evade tariffs,” Mr. McCaul said, recounting advice he said he had received from a Ukrainian sanctions expert during a recent trip to Kyiv.

That argument ultimately persuaded lawmakers in both parties.

Representative French Hill, Republican of Arkansas and the chairman of the Financial Services Committee, said the measure could have been better designed and warned that its tariffs could harm American trading partners. Still, he urged passage, saying that Congress needed to send “a loud, resounding message to the Kremlin.”

Representative Steny H. Hoyer, Democrat of Maryland and another key negotiator, made a similar case. Mr. Trump, he said, already claimed expansive tariff authority, while the legislation before Congress specifically directed economic pressure toward countries helping sustain Russia’s war.

“This is something we can do,” Mr. Hoyer said.

The vote came as the fighting in Ukraine has intensified and Russia has increasingly struck the transportation and energy infrastructure.

On Sunday, a Russian drone struck a passenger train near the Polish border, shortly after a train carrying former Prime Minister Boris Johnson of Britain and other European officials had traveled through the area. The former C.I.A. director David Petraeus was at the station when the drone hit. No deaths were reported, and it was unclear whether the rail station was the intended target of the strike. Russia said it was targeting infrastructure used to transport military cargo from Europe.

“They just bombed the train that goes from Kyiv to Warsaw,” said Mr. McCaul. “We do not have time to wait.”
