item.title: The Midterm Sprint Has Begun. Here’s Your Guide.
item.description:
Last-minute super PAC money is cascading into House and Senate battlegrounds. Some mail ballots are already on their way to voters. Heck, President Trump is spending this evening campaigning in a swing state.

The midterms are here. And tonight, we’re going to break down the state of the race.

With less than seven weeks to go, the ambient political environment — the vibes, if you will — are not great for Republicans. Amid persistent inflation, an unpopular war and low presidential approval ratings, The Times’s Nate Cohn sees comparisons to the “blue wave” of 2018, which delivered control of the House back to Democrats.

Strategists and elected officials in both parties see control of the House as Democrats’ to lose. Control of the Senate remains something of a tossup.

Republicans have found themselves playing defense in places they’re not used to worrying about (like Kansas, which we looked at Monday). But the specifics of this year’s contested races — including the fact that so many are happening in red states — may yet buoy Republicans.

If I had to boil the midterms down to a single question, it would be this: Will the bad vibes for Republicans overwhelm their structural advantages?

Here’s what to know.

A poll released yesterday by The Times and Siena University tells the story of what’s going well for Democrats right now. It found that likely voters favored Democratic candidates over Republican ones by 9 percentage points in their congressional districts — and that the president’s approval rating is mired at 38 percent.

There are a few more findings that illustrate how Republicans grew so vulnerable.

Trump has lost the public’s trust on the economy, which is the issue that propelled him back to office in 2024. Only 28 percent of voters said they approved of how Trump has managed matters related to affordability. And even his most loyal supporters — white voters without college degrees — disapprove of his handling of cost of living.

The Iran War is unpopular. Seventy-seven percent of independents disapprove of Trump’s handling of it, as do nearly a quarter of people who said they voted for Trump in 2024.

It’s not just Trump. The poll found that voters see Republicans broadly as more extreme, more elitist and more corrupt than Democrats.

Democrats always knew they were going to face a daunting Senate map this fall. To win control, they need to flip four seats currently held by Republicans, while maintaining their hold on seats in two states that Trump won in 2024: Georgia and Michigan.

That Senate control is even up for grabs — and that the battleground map is as broad as it is — reflects the stiff headwinds against Republicans I’ve just laid out. But clinching it will require Democrats to muscle through in states where Republicans hold plenty of advantages.

Think of the races as falling into four different buckets.

The purple states leaning toward Democrats: Party leaders are increasingly confident that Senator Jon Ossoff, a Georgia Democrat, will hold onto his seat in the face of a challenge from Representative Mike Collins. In North Carolina, former Gov. Roy Cooper has maintained a consistent polling lead over Michael Whatley, the former chairman of the Republican National Committee.

The red states becoming battlegrounds: Democratic candidates are posting significant fund-raising hauls and strong polling numbers in Ohio, Texas, Alaska and Iowa, which is forcing Republicans to spend heavily to defend their seats in all four states. There’s also an independent candidate mounting a serious challenge in Nebraska.

The seats Republicans want to flip: Strong Republican recruitment has turned the Senate race in New Hampshire, where the Democrat Jeanne Shaheen is retiring, into what many observers consider a tossup. In Michigan, Republicans hope voters will see Dr. Abdul El-Sayed as too liberal for the swing state.

And there’s Maine: Democrats had a rough time picking a nominee to take on Senator Susan Collins, a Republican. But now, the race between her and Troy Jackson looks close.

Then there’s the House. Republicans worked to stave off their losses with aggressive redistricting, which helped the party protect as many as 11 seats. But Democrats believe that the political environment will allow them to be competitive in districts Trump won by double digits in 2024.

For months, even the most bullish Democrats would privately admit to harboring deep worry about spending by outside groups that support Republicans. The last few days show you why: The gusher of cash from President Trump’s super PAC, MAGA Inc., has arrived.

Last night, The Times reported that MAGA Inc. had, over the prior 10 days, reserved a whopping $138 million in advertising in a last-ditch effort to save Republicans’ control of Congress. The top destinations for that money, my colleague Teddy Schleifer tells me, are Senate races in Michigan ($18.2 million), Ohio ($15.1 million), Alaska ($11.3 million), New Hampshire and Texas ($10.8 million apiece).

Democratic Senate candidates have often outraised their opponents. But spending like that has helped Republicans open up a $370 million advantage over Democrats when it comes to advertising this cycle, according to tracking by AdImpact — a gap that could grow between now and November.

The Inbox

I want to hear from you, On Politics readers. What interesting, quirky, super-specific issue has become the biggest deal on your ballot? It could be playing out in a local race — or maybe it’s something you think could shape a statewide contest. Has never-ending highway construction turned neighbors into enemies? Is there an overabundance of moose that needs to come under control?

Let me know at onpolitics@nytimes.com, and I may feature it in a future newsletter. The weirder, the better.

The Supreme Court told Trump this week that he could not use the Postal Service to screen mail-in ballots, blocking his administration’s most apparent attempt to change how this year’s elections are run. But that was far from their only effort. Here’s what else we’re keeping an eye on as Election Day approaches:

The agents: Kash Patel, the F.B.I. director, told senators yesterday that he was open to sending his agents to polling places — even though, by law, armed federal officers can’t be deployed to election sites.

The machines: The homeland security secretary, Markwayne Mullin, has pushed for an investigation into whether a commonly used voting machine can be trusted. The request, our reporters noted, could lay the groundwork for post-election claims that some votes are invalid.

The voter rolls: Federal agents are scouring states’ voter registries searching for noncitizens. Last week, the Justice Department sent threatening letters to at least 30 election officials in states that refused to hand over voters’ information.

The safeguards: Trump has gutted the government’s election security agency — which he himself created in 2018. Without that agency’s help, lawmakers of both parties worry that the midterms will be more susceptible to cyberattacks and foreign influence campaigns.

Catch Me Up

The Federal Reserve, hoping to tame inflation, raised interest rates today for the first time since 2023. The move is likely to put Kevin Warsh, the new Fed chair, in an awkward spot with Trump, who frequently lashed out at his predecessor over his refusal to lower rates.

The Cook Political Report, which assesses the state of political races, shifted its rating of the New Hampshire Senate contest from “lean Democratic” to “tossup.”

The Kennedy Center is now closed to the public. The center’s board voted to shutter it on Tuesday, shortly after a federal judge ruled that Trump could not inscribe his name on the building.

This year’s primaries were full of candidate switch-ups, nation-shaking upsets and debate debacles. Before you read Tim Balk’s roller-coaster look back at those chaotic months, test your memory with a quiz question.

In August, Tom Smith won his Republican primary for a House seat in Michigan, despite the fact that he …

Ended his campaign a month earlier

Switched parties a day before the election

Ran his entire campaign from Paris

Never registered to run in the first place

Called himself “Ohio State’s biggest fan”

Choose your answer, and we’ll take you to Tim’s story and let you know if you’re right. (We’ve also made it free to read.)

item.title: Trump Wanted Canada as the 51st State. He Ended Up Pushing It Toward the European Union.
item.description:
Early in his second term, President Trump wanted Canada so entwined with the United States that he even set out to make it the 51st state. Instead, he has driven Canada into the arms of the European Union, after antagonizing the Canadians for months, taunting the country’s prime minister and waging a relentless trade war.

The invitation by the European Union on Wednesday for Canada to become an “associate member” is a sign of the knock-on effects of Mr. Trump’s brand of diplomacy, which often involves threatening countries that once were considered America’s closest friends.

And even if the gesture by the E.U. ends up being more symbolic than substantive, it shows how Mr. Trump is upending global relationships in ways that will be difficult to undo.

“We should see this action from Canada and the E.U. as a direct consequence of Trump’s actions and rhetoric,” said James Batchik, a deputy director at the Atlantic Council’s Europe Center. “The rhetoric around making Canada the 51st state, and the threats against Greenland, which are still highly, highly, controversial and remembered in Brussels, are really reminders for both sides that the United States is not necessarily that trusted ally that it once was.”

At every turn, Mr. Trump’s bullying approach to Canada has appeared to backfire. His trade war stirred up trouble for embattled Republicans in swing states, endangering G.O.P. control of the Senate. And his hostility toward Canadian leaders helped surge the country’s struggling liberal party, no friend of Mr. Trump’s, to electoral victory.

President Trump responded to the E.U.’s overture to Canada with fury while speaking to reporters Wednesday night.

“Canada’s been a terrible trade partner,” he said. “No, I don’t see that. If they do that, if I think it’s at all a hostile act, I will put very serious tariffs or stop trading with Europe on many things. So, if they do that, if Europe does that, with a bad intention — if it’s a good intention, that’s fine — if it’s a bad intention we’ll put very heavy tariffs on Europe, which is a possibility.”

Mr. Trump’s battle with Canada is part of his striking focus on a Western Hemisphere that recent presidents, typically consumed with the Middle East and Asia, have often neglected.

Mr. Trump, emboldened after a U.S. operation that toppled the leader of Venezuela, has set his sights this year on other countries in the Western Hemisphere. He has applied massive economic pressure against Cuba and proposed a “friendly takeover.” He has threatened to seize the Panama Canal and to wrest the North American island of Greenland from Denmark.

In an update of the Monroe Doctrine, the 1823 foundational statement of U.S. claims over the Western Hemisphere, with what he called the “Trump Corollary,” Mr. Trump formally declared that “the American people — not foreign nations nor globalist institutions — will always control their own destiny in our hemisphere.”

(Mr. Trump often refers to the concept as the “Donroe Doctrine,” named after himself.)

In the cases of Cuba and Venezuela, Mr. Trump’s policies are led by Secretary of State Marco Rubio, a Cuban-American whose interest in Latin America is driven by his strong anti-socialist ideology. Mr. Rubio has shown far less public enthusiasm for Mr. Trump’s territorial claims than he does for democratizing the region.

But Mr. Trump’s fixation with Canada is mainly rooted in trade and economics, not territory or politics.

The president started his second term threatening Canada’s previous leader, Justin Trudeau, whom Mr. Trump publicly derided, with unilaterally scrapping agreements that have governed the relationship between the neighboring countries for over a century.

He has imposed tariffs on Canada, which with Mexico is one of America’s two top trading partners, that are crippling some of Canada’s key economic sectors, such as autos, steel, aluminum and lumber.

In part because of Mr. Trump’s attacks, Canadians rallied around Mr. Trudeau’s successor, Prime Minister Mark Carney, who positioned himself as a fighter against the American president. This year, Mr. Carney delivered a speech in Davos, Switzerland, in which he called for a new world order, no longer led by America, prompting global political and corporate leaders in the audience to rise from their seats for a rare standing ovation.

“The middle powers must act together because if we’re not at the table, we’re on the menu,” Mr. Carney said.

Liana Fix, a senior fellow for Europe at the Council on Foreign Relations, said it wasn’t clear what Canada becoming an “associate member” of the E.U. would mean, beyond trade and defense agreements already in place. But Canada and the European Union will meet for a summit at the end of October, when they are expected to lay out more concrete ideas.

Ursula von der Leyen, the president of the European Union, has said Canada and Europe could work more closely together on the Arctic, their defense industrial bases and critical minerals.

“The E.U. wants to make a statement that the middle powers have a say and will not be bullied by the Trump administration,” Ms. Fix said.

The reaction of Canada and European leaders is perhaps unsurprising, given Mr. Trump’s penchant for attacking allies and playing nice with historic rivals, Mr. Batchik said.

“Donald Trump has been pulling his punches toward some of our adversaries, top of mind Russia and China, and doubling down and taking a rather gleeful approach to needling our previous would-be allies,” Mr. Batchik said. “You’re starting to see many across Europe taking that to heart and saying, OK, if that’s truly the case, if that’s how the United States is going to treat its allies, they’re just going to look elsewhere.”

It could end up being “a generational turn away from the United States,” he said, “or at least will take a significant amount of energy and time to repair these relations.”

Erica L. Green contributed.

item.title: House Passes Bill Taking Aim at Data Center Electricity Costs
item.description:
The House on Wednesday overwhelmingly passed a bipartisan bill that encourages state utility regulators to insulate consumers from rising energy costs tied to data centers, as members of Congress rush to address a voter outcry over the rapid advance of artificial intelligence.

It was unclear whether the legislation, introduced by Representatives Gabe Evans, Republican of Colorado, and Kathy Castor, Democrat of Florida, would have its intended effect. The bill would direct state utility regulators to consider adopting federal rules requiring data centers to cover any higher costs associated with their large-scale power use. But under current law, Congress cannot force state regulators to follow federal standards when they are setting electricity rates.

Still, as the boom in data center construction has become a potent issue in November’s midterm elections, lawmakers in both parties have been eager to have a legislative achievement that they could cite on the campaign trail. It would still have to pass the Senate and be signed by President Trump before it could become law.

Across the country, Americans in both parties are concerned about rising electricity prices and water use. Data centers, the large complexes of servers that are crucial to powering A.I. development, have become the most visible avatar of voters’ fears over the growth of artificial intelligence and the power of big tech companies.

That issue took on new political urgency this week, after concerns over the safety of A.I. emerged into wider view and key tech leaders began calling for a slowdown in the pace of development.

Lawmakers in both parties have called on Congress to impose guardrails on artificial intelligence, though there is no clear bipartisan consensus on how to do so, and President Trump has rejected calls for regulation. Speaker Mike Johnson said on Tuesday that he and the president would convene a meeting with A.I. executives at the White House next week.

When asked about their plans to address the issue, some House Republicans pointed to the utility legislation, which does not address A.I. safety concerns. The measure mirrors a voluntary pledge that tech executives made at the White House earlier this year, when they promised to shoulder a larger share of the energy costs associated with data centers.

“It makes sure that the ratepayers are protected as you’re building out A.I. infrastructure,” said Representative Steve Scalise of Louisiana, the No. 2 Republican. “That it’s got to be supported by the local community, and that it’s not going to adversely impact ratepayers.”

Wednesday’s vote, 417 to 3, reflected the increasingly bipartisan nature of the data center backlash and a growing concern among Republicans that they are particularly vulnerable on the issue after their signature domestic policy bill included tax breaks that benefited developers of data centers. It also marked a turnabout from just a year ago, when almost all House Republicans backed a version of that measure that put a moratorium on any state regulation of A.I., though the provision was later stripped by the Senate.

With the House leaving town on Wednesday until after Election Day, this week was lawmakers’ last chance to pass a bill showing they were responsive to voters’ concerns about data centers.

Mr. Evans, who introduced the utility bill, is among the most politically vulnerable Republicans in the House. It is unclear whether the Senate will take up the legislation before October, when it is scheduled to recess until after November’s elections. Its version of the bill was put forward by Senator Jon Husted, a Republican in a competitive race in Ohio in which Democrats have sought to make data centers a central issue.

A poll conducted this month by The New York Times and Siena University found that 61 percent of voters said they opposed the construction of data centers and were about split on which party was better positioned to address it, with a considerable bloc saying they did not know which side to trust.

When Republicans last year passed their sweeping tax and spending cut bill, they expanded significant tax advantages for businesses for research costs and new investments. They also adjusted a tax break program meant to encourage development in poorer areas so that it would incentivize more development in rural areas.

Democrats have argued that those provisions have helped technology companies looking to build new data centers, and they have accused Republicans of being indifferent to voters’ worries that such construction is raising their electricity costs and changing their neighborhoods.

“Unfortunately, these very real concerns are repeatedly swept to the sidelines, minimized or ridiculed by President Trump and Republican congressional leaders,” said Representative Frank Pallone Jr., Democrat of New Jersey.

Some Republicans have argued that regulations on artificial intelligence would hinder America’s ability to stay ahead of China in developing the technology. On the House floor, Mr. Evans presented his bill as a way to allow for data center development while ensuring that states had a mechanism to address implications for communities.

The bill, he said, “keeps costs low for Americans and helps us build the energy backbone required to compete and win in the A.I. race.”

item.title: A Sky Full of Hazards: Above L.A., the Crowded World of a Helicopter
item.description:
They swoop, dip and hover over traffic-choked streets to capture bird’s-eye views of sprawling cities. They can be indispensable to newscasts that are capturing the chaos of the day: multicar collisions, dramatic storm rescues or fugitives on the lam.

To do all that, news helicopters must navigate the many hazards of a crowded airspace, like drones, birds and towering buildings. But after three people were killed on Tuesday when a helicopter plummeted to the ground in Los Angeles, an old question gained new urgency: Can they operate safely?

Investigators on Wednesday were only beginning to comb through clues at the site of the blackened wreckage in the San Fernando Valley neighborhood of Chatsworth. The cause of the crash was unknown.

But the disaster put the dangers of aerial news gathering into stark relief, at a time when the potential of other monitoring technologies, like drones, seems to be accelerating by the day. Perhaps nowhere is this more evident than in Los Angeles, where news helicopters are considered critical in covering the city’s vast expanse.

The pilots of these helicopters must keep their heads on a swivel. While the flights are regulated by the Federal Aviation Administration, which sets standards for matters like altitude and communication, the pilots do not have air traffic controllers to guide them. And there is no limit to the number of helicopters that can fly in any one area.

Because of those factors, helicopters responding to a disaster — which may be operated by police departments, hospitals or news outlets — must be in constant communication with one another, said Hassan Shahidi, president of the Flight Safety Foundation, a nonprofit that provides safety guidance to the aviation industry.

A spokesman from the F.A.A. said that helicopter pilots communicate through radio to inform one another of their whereabouts, adding that this method has been effective for decades.

According to F.A.A. data, Los Angeles County has among the highest number of registered rotorcraft — a category that includes helicopters and other aircraft with rotors to generate lift — in the nation.

Stu Mundel, an aerial photojournalist for Fox11 who has worked in the field for about a quarter century, said he had experienced two helicopter engine failures during his career, along with other frightening moments in the air.

“I can tell you many times where the thought literally goes through my mind, ‘Huh. So this is how I die,’” he said. Still, he added, risk is part of the job for helicopter pilots, and the crash on Tuesday would not change that perspective.

Helicopter reporting is not as common as it used to be. The costs of fuel, labor and maintenance make it increasingly out of reach for many local news outlets with declining funds.

But reporters still use helicopters in big cities like Los Angeles and New York. Even so, many are operated not by news stations, but by aviation companies that consolidate costs by serving multiple outlets.

Some stations use drones for aerial footage, which are far cheaper to operate. But experts say that because of the country’s current regulations on those aircraft, they cannot compare to helicopters.

The F.A.A. has regulations for airspace and restrictions on flying over people. Local and state governments can control where you can take off and can enact a complicated array of restrictions on issues like privacy and surveillance.

News crews that use drones must be certified under an F.A.A. rule known as Part 107, which require operators to register their drones and keep them in their line of sight whenever they are airborne.

That limits the distance such drones can be sent ahead of a TV truck to respond quickly to a scene. Without additional authorizations, drones are limited to certain designated airspaces, must weigh less than 55 pounds — including cameras, lights and other cargo — and fly no higher than 400 feet off the ground, except in the vicinity of certain structures.

Drone flights can be further limited by, among other reasons, temporary flight restrictions, weather, time of day or minimum visibility requirements.

The best drones for reliable, steady video footage are not limited only by federal regulations, but also by their batteries, said Matt Waite, a journalism professor who studies drone use in reporting at the University of Nebraska-Lincoln.

“You can’t fly for more than about a mile,” Mr. Waite said. “You can’t fly more than about 20 to 40 minutes. If it’s windy, God be with you. There are just a lot of limitations to this.”

A helicopter, on the other hand, can often get to a location more quickly and stay there longer. Michael Izquierdo, the chief pilot of Beverly Hills Aerials, a drone-filming company in Los Angeles, said a helicopter could fly for hours. “It can go at a higher speed; it can carry a bigger camera,” he said.

Joel Smith, a helicopter pilot and the founder of HERO Aviation, a safety management company, said that major news events like fires can draw 15 or 20 helicopters, including both responders and news outlets, to the same area at once.

“It sounds like it’s chaotic, but it’s really not,” he said. “It’s actually a very orchestrated, organized flow of traffic.”

Often, helicopters arriving at a scene operate in what is known as a stack, Mr. Smith said, with law enforcement and other responding agencies flying low, up to about 500 feet, and command helicopters flying above them. News crews can fly their helicopters even higher, he said, or laterally farther away.

Crashes like the one in Los Angeles are rare, but not unheard of. Since 2000, there have been at least eight other deadly crashes involving news-gathering helicopters, and at least 16 people have died.

While helicopter safety has been improving in recent years, the risk of accidents in rotorcraft still outpaces that of airplanes, particularly when it comes to ones that result in fatalities.

According to data compiled by the Aircraft Owners and Pilots Association, a nonprofit trade group representing general aviation, commercial helicopters recorded an accident rate of 2.66 incidents per 100,000 flight hours in 2023. That is more than twice as high as comparable accident rates for fixed-wing commercial aircraft.

Helicopter accidents generally occur most frequently when the aircraft collide with obstacles or other low-altitude hazards. Equipment failures, weather events and pilot errors, particularly when visibility is low, can also play a role. But sometimes the culprit can be something unpredictable, like a bird. Last year, a tour helicopter that crashed into the Hudson River in New York, killing six, was most likely struck by a flock of geese, according to National Transportation Safety Board documents.

Two of the people who died in the crash on Tuesday were in the helicopter: The reporter Eliana Moreno and the pilot George Marciniw had been flying together since 2023, according to the television news station NBC4.

The third person who died was a pedestrian, the authorities said.

As is often the case for helicopter news crews, Ms. Moreno and Mr. Marciniw did not work directly for NBC4. The station said that its NewsChopper4 had been operated by Angel City Air, an aerial news-gathering company based in Los Angeles and serving multiple outlets.

The company is a division of Welk Aviation, which did not respond to requests for comment on Wednesday. Its website says that Angel City Air has 15 years of experience operating news helicopters in Los Angeles, and it describes the city as “one of the most competitive aerial news-gathering environments in the world.”

Shawn Hubler, Josh Haner and Steven Rich contributed reporting. Kitty Bennett contributed research.
